title: Count Number of Nice Subarrays
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting odd numbers in every subarray directly versus reducing to parities and applying the Subarray Sum Equals K prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the number of "nice" subarrays, where a nice subarray is one containing exactly k odd numbers.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given nums and k, count every contiguous subarray that contains exactly k odd numbers, regardless of how many even numbers it also contains.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Stretches With Exactly k Red Marbles
blocks.text: Picture a row of marbles, some red (odd) and some blue (even), and needing to count every contiguous stretch of marbles containing exactly k red ones, no matter how many blue marbles are mixed in.

blocks.caption: Replacing each number with 0 or 1 turns this into Subarray Sum Equals K

blocks.text: The subarrays [1,1,2,1] and [1,2,1,1] each contain exactly 3 odd numbers, giving a count of 2.
There are 16 subarrays containing exactly 2 odd numbers.
Edge case: no odd numbers exist and k is positive
If there are fewer than k odd numbers in the entire array, no subarray can qualify, and the count is 0.
Before checking every subarray for its odd count, notice that only whether each number is odd or even actually matters, its exact value does not.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Replacing every odd number with 1 and every even number with 0 turns "exactly k odd numbers in a subarray" into "this subarray of 0s and 1s sums to exactly k."

Observation 2: That is exactly the Subarray Sum Equals K problem, solved with a running prefix sum and a hashmap counting how many times each prefix sum has occurred.

Observation 3: At each position, the number of valid subarrays ENDING there equals how many earlier prefix sums are exactly k less than the current one.

Observation 4: Accumulating that count at every position, while updating the hashmap, gives the total count in one pass.
This leads directly to reusing the prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique on the sequence of parities instead of the raw numbers.
Check every subarray directly, counting its odd numbers, and tally those with exactly k.

items: For every starting index i and ending index j (i at most j), count the odd numbers in nums[i..j] directly.
If that count equals k, increment the running total.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: count odd numbers in every subarray directly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every starting index restarts its own odd count and extends outward, checking the count at every ending position.
No information about parities is shared or reused between different starting points.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Start i","Odd count reaches k at end index","Counted"],"rows":[["0","end 3 ([1,1,2,1])","yes"],["1","end 4 ([1,2,1,1])","yes"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), every pair of start and end indices is examined.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: restarting the odd count for every starting index repeats work that a single running prefix count, combined with a hashmap, could share across every position.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-scanning per start index is wasteful: only the DIFFERENCE in odd count between two positions determines whether the subarray between them is nice, and that difference can be derived from two running counts instead of a fresh scan.

What is the exact condition: a subarray from index i plus 1 to j is nice exactly when the running odd count up to j minus the running odd count up to i equals k.

How to count this efficiently: as the running count grows one position at a time, look up how many earlier positions had a running count equal to (current count minus k), using a hashmap, and add that to the answer.

The core idea: maintain a running count of odd numbers, and a hashmap of how many times each running count value has occurred so far, exactly the Subarray Sum Equals K technique applied to parities.

Maintain a running count of odd numbers seen so far, and a hashmap mapping each running count value to how many times it has occurred, starting with count 0 occurring once (before any elements). At each position, add the hashmap's entry for (current count minus k) to the answer, then record the current count in the hashmap.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: running count plus a hashmap, the Subarray Sum Equals K technique

codes.python:
def number_of_subarrays(nums, k):
    count = {0: 1}                       # running-count value -> how many times seen
    odd, result = 0, 0
    for x in nums:
        odd += x % 2                       # running count of odd numbers so far
        result += count.get(odd - k, 0)    # subarrays ending here with exactly k odds
        count[odd] = count.get(odd, 0) + 1
    return result

blocks.text: A subarray is nice exactly when the running odd count at its end minus the running odd count just before its start equals k. Recording every running count seen so far in a hashmap lets each new position immediately find how many earlier starting points make the difference equal exactly k, adding all of them to the answer in one lookup.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass with O(1) average hashmap operations.
Space: O(n), for the hashmap of running counts.

blocks.text: The key insight is recognizing that "exactly k odd numbers" is the same shape as "subarray sums to k," once every number is reduced to just its parity, turning this into a direct application of the prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique.

items: Not recognizing the reduction to parities and instead trying to track odd/even values directly in a more complicated way.
Forgetting to seed the hashmap with count 0 occurring once, which represents the empty prefix before any elements.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the reduction, "replace each number with its parity, then this is Subarray Sum Equals K," is the fastest way to show this problem was recognized as a variant of a well-known pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "does this remind you of another problem", think: reduce numbers to their parity, and this becomes Subarray Sum Equals K.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) space. The optimized prefix-count-plus-hashmap approach runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

items: Pattern: reduce to parities, then apply the Subarray Sum Equals K prefix-sum-plus-hashmap technique.
Core Idea: a subarray has exactly k odd numbers exactly when the difference between two running odd-counts equals k, countable with a hashmap in one pass.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized hashmap.
Most Important Observation: only the parity of each number matters, reducing this directly to a well-known prefix-sum pattern.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the reduction to Subarray Sum Equals K is recognized.
One line memory trick: parity plus a hashmap, exactly Subarray Sum Equals K in disguise.
